inputs.need:
I am the lead oncology pharmacist at a regional cancer centre that treats about 2,600 new patients a year. About 480 patients a year now start oral anticancer agents at home: capecitabine, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, PARP inhibitors, abiraterone and others. These patients see the oncologist every four to twelve weeks, and in between they manage complex schedules, dose holidays and side effects on their own. Last year 17 percent of patients starting an oral agent had an unplanned admission within 90 days, about half of them for toxicity such as diarrhoea, hand-foot syndrome or neutropenic fever, and our dispensing records suggest that about one in five collect their repeat supplies late.

Our drug and therapeutics committee has asked whether we should fund a pharmacist-led oral chemotherapy follow-up service: a pharmacist consultation before the first cycle, telephone toxicity and adherence checks at days 7, 14 and 28, and a pharmacist review before each new supply. The committee wants the evidence in about four months, with what the service would take in staff and money and what it might save, because the funding round closes in February 2027. A full evidence synthesis is not possible in that time, so I would like to run a rapid review.

The questions I think matter are these. Does pharmacist-led follow-up improve adherence to oral anticancer agents, and how was adherence measured? Does it reduce unplanned admissions or severe toxicity? What does it do to dose intensity, since earlier dose reductions for toxicity could protect patients but also reduce how much treatment they receive? How much pharmacist time does it take per patient? What does such a service need in money, and what is saved in admissions? And what do patients think of it? I know adherence can be measured in very different ways (pill counts, refill data, electronic caps, self-report) that give different answers, and that most studies are small.

Practical points. Two pharmacists can each give six hours a week to the review until the end of January, and our library can run searches. We cannot pay for translation. We want to include reports from other cancer centres and health technology assessment agencies, not only journal articles. The committee has asked that we separate evidence about adherence from evidence about harms and money, because last time a single summary figure was misleading. Our own admission and dispensing data are context only; they are not part of the review, and they cannot be shared outside the centre. We also need to be honest about what a rapid review cannot do: one screener for most records, and no full appraisal of every study.

Finally, the committee chair asked that the summary say clearly who the evidence does not cover: older patients living alone, patients who do not speak English, and patients far from the centre who cannot easily come in for a pharmacist review. About a fifth of our patients live more than 100 kilometres away, and a small but growing number start treatment with an interpreter present, so this matters for how a service would be designed as well as for whether it is funded. If the evidence turns out to be too thin for a firm answer, I would rather the committee hear that plainly, with the gaps named, than receive a confident summary built on a few small studies.
inputs.constraints: No research budget. Two pharmacists for six hours a week each until 29 January 2027; the committee's funding round closes on 15 February 2027. Library searches are available; there is no budget for translation, so only English reports are eligible. Most records will be screened by one reviewer, with a second reviewer checking a 20 percent sample. Evidence about adherence must be reported separately from evidence about harms and about staff time and money; no single summary figure combining them. The centre's own admission and dispensing data are context only and cannot leave the centre. No contact with patients or prescribers for the review. The summary for the committee must be no longer than six pages plus appendices and must state which patient groups the evidence does not cover. Reports must be dated 2010 or later. Conference abstracts are eligible only when they report outcomes not available elsewhere. Any cost figure must be shown with the year and currency of the original report and must not be converted or inflated without stating the method. The review protocol, including these shortcuts, must be filed with the committee secretary before screening starts. Draft tables may be shared with the committee chair once, in the week of 11 January 2027.

response.subtitle: Adherence, harms and dose intensity, and staff time and money, reported as separate strands
response.statement: About 480 patients a year start oral anticancer agents at the centre; 17 percent have an unplanned admission within 90 days, half for toxicity, and about one in five collect repeat supplies late. The drug and therapeutics committee must decide by February 2027 whether to fund a pharmacist-led follow-up service. A rapid review will summarise evidence on adherence (by measurement method), unplanned admissions and severe toxicity, dose intensity, pharmacist time, costs and patients' views, reported as separate strands.
response.whoAffected: Adults starting oral anticancer agents at home, especially older patients living alone, patients who need interpreters and patients far from the centre; oncology pharmacists and oncologists; the committee.
response.whatHurts: Toxicity recognised late leads to admissions and interrupted treatment; poor adherence can reduce benefit; a service funded on a misleading single figure could divert pharmacist time from other patients.
response.currentPractice: Oncology review every four to twelve weeks with no structured pharmacist follow-up between visits.
response.whyNow: The committee's funding round closes on 15 February 2027 and it asked for a report by 20 January.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients taking cancer treatment at home have toxicity recognised early and keep receiving the treatment they need, wherever they live and whatever language they speak.
response.summary: Problem framed as a rapid review for a funding decision, with separate strands for adherence, harms, and time and costs.

steps.query: pharmacist-led follow-up oral anticancer agents adherence toxicity unplanned admission dose intensity cost

records.title: Pharmacist-led follow-up for patients starting oral anticancer agents: a randomised trial of adherence and unplanned admissions
records.authors: Moreno-Achterberg L, Osei-Whitfield K, Tanaka-Brandt R
records.abstract: We randomly allocated 212 adults starting capecitabine or a tyrosine kinase inhibitor to pharmacist-led follow-up, with a consultation before the first cycle and telephone checks at days 7, 14 and 28, or to usual oncology follow-up. At 12 weeks, adherence by pill count was 91 percent with pharmacist follow-up and 79 percent with usual care. Unplanned admissions within 90 days occurred in 9 percent and 15 percent respectively, a difference compatible with chance. Relative dose intensity was 0.87 and 0.92. The trial was not powered for admissions or toxicity.

records.title: Costs and savings of an oral chemotherapy pharmacy clinic: a single-centre budget analysis
records.abstract: We estimated the annual cost of a pharmacist-led oral chemotherapy clinic for 400 patients and the admissions it might avert. The clinic cost about 118,000 a year in pharmacist time and overheads. Using admission rates before and after the clinic started and an average cost of 7,400 per toxicity admission, averted admissions were valued at between 64,000 and 141,000 a year depending on assumptions. The before-after admission rates were not adjusted for case mix, and costs to patients were not included. The authors present the result as a budget range, not a net saving.

records.title: Measuring adherence to oral anticancer agents: agreement between pill counts, pharmacy refill data and electronic caps
records.abstract: In 96 patients taking oral anticancer agents, we compared three adherence measures over 12 weeks. Mean adherence was 93 percent by pharmacy refill data, 88 percent by pill count and 81 percent by electronic caps. Refill data overestimated adherence compared with electronic caps by 8 to 12 percentage points, largely because patients who collected supplies on time did not always take doses as scheduled. Self-report was highest of all at 97 percent. The authors recommend that studies state which measure they use and avoid comparing results across measures.

records.title: Telephone toxicity checks by oncology pharmacists and dose intensity of capecitabine
records.abstract: We compared 164 patients receiving capecitabine with pharmacist telephone toxicity checks against 171 patients treated before the checks were introduced. Grade 3 or worse diarrhoea or hand-foot syndrome fell from 21 to 13 percent. Dose reductions were made earlier and more often with the checks, and relative dose intensity over the first three cycles was 0.86 against 0.91. Survival was not assessed. The authors note that earlier dose reductions may trade toxicity for dose intensity and that the balance needs longer follow-up.

records.title: Patients' views of pharmacist support when taking cancer treatment at home
records.abstract: We talked with 26 patients taking oral anticancer agents at home about pharmacist telephone follow-up. Patients valued having a named person to call about side effects, and several said they would otherwise have waited until the next clinic visit to report problems. Some found repeated calls intrusive once they felt confident. Patients living alone and those with limited English described the most difficulty managing complex schedules, but they were under-represented in the study. The authors suggest tailoring the frequency of calls to each patient.

records.title: Interventions to support adherence to oral anticancer agents: a review of 31 studies
records.authors: Oyelaran-Petersen H, McAllister-Iwu S, Brennan-Dube A
records.abstract: We identified 31 studies of interventions to support adherence to oral anticancer agents, including 12 randomised trials. Pharmacist-led interventions were the most common. Effects on adherence were inconsistent, partly because adherence was measured in at least six different ways, and effects were largest when measured by self-report. Only 7 studies reported unplanned admissions and 4 reported costs. Few studies included patients over 75 or patients who did not speak the local language. The authors call for standard adherence measures and reporting of harms.

records.title: Unplanned admissions within 90 days of starting oral anticancer therapy in a regional cancer network
records.abstract: Across five cancer centres, we followed 3,120 patients starting oral anticancer agents. Eighteen percent had an unplanned admission within 90 days, and 49 percent of these admissions were attributed to treatment toxicity, most often diarrhoea, neutropenic fever or hand-foot syndrome. Risk was higher in patients over 75, patients living alone and those living more than 100 kilometres from the centre. The authors suggest that early follow-up should prioritise these groups and that services should be designed for patients who cannot easily travel.

records.title: Pharmacist time per patient in oral chemotherapy follow-up programmes: a multi-centre time study
records.abstract: We timed pharmacist activities in oral chemotherapy follow-up programmes at four cancer centres over eight weeks. Pharmacist time per patient over the first 12 weeks of treatment was a median of 2.6 hours, ranging from 1.4 to 4.1 hours between centres, with most time spent on the first consultation and on toxicity calls. Centres that used structured call scripts spent less time per call. The authors estimate that one full-time pharmacist can follow about 450 new patients a year alongside other duties.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records of the 19 hits the search reported, appraised at abstract level; 11 hits were not ingested and are unappraised. Adherence: one trial found higher pill-count adherence with pharmacist follow-up, but measures disagree by up to 12 points and a review found inconsistent effects. Harms: severe toxicity fell after pharmacist toxicity checks in a historical comparison, with lower dose intensity as a balancing concern; admissions did not differ clearly in the trial. Time and money: about 2.6 pharmacist hours per patient over 12 weeks; one centre's budget range for averted admissions overlapped the clinic's cost. Patients valued a named pharmacist, and the groups at highest risk were least studied.
response.gradeRationale: One small trial, historical comparisons, one budget analysis and a review of inconsistent studies; low certainty for adherence and harms, very low for costs, and incomplete because 11 hits were not ingested.
response.summary: Eight of 19 hits appraised; seven claims in separate strands; certainty low.

response.finer: Feasible in four months with two pharmacists part-time and library support; interesting and relevant to the funding decision; novel only as a local synthesis; ethical with no participants.
response.summary: One effects question with harms as the primary strand, and one time and money question kept separate.

response.rationale: The committee needs a synthesis in four months, which a rapid review can deliver with stated shortcuts: one screener with a 20 percent check, English only, and abstract-level appraisal for most records. The evidence is narrow and heterogeneous: adherence measures disagree (c2), harms and dose intensity move together (c3, c4), and costs rest on one budget range (c5). The review is narrowed to pharmacist-led follow-up in adults starting oral agents and reports its strands separately. store.title: Pharmacist-led follow-up for patients starting oral anticancer agents: a rapid review for a funding decision
store.problem.rawNeed:
I am the lead oncology pharmacist at a regional cancer centre that treats about 2,600 new patients a year. About 480 patients a year now start oral anticancer agents at home: capecitabine, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, PARP inhibitors, abiraterone and others. These patients see the oncologist every four to twelve weeks, and in between they manage complex schedules, dose holidays and side effects on their own. Last year 17 percent of patients starting an oral agent had an unplanned admission within 90 days, about half of them for toxicity such as diarrhoea, hand-foot syndrome or neutropenic fever, and our dispensing records suggest that about one in five collect their repeat supplies late.

Our drug and therapeutics committee has asked whether we should fund a pharmacist-led oral chemotherapy follow-up service: a pharmacist consultation before the first cycle, telephone toxicity and adherence checks at days 7, 14 and 28, and a pharmacist review before each new supply. The committee wants the evidence in about four months, with what the service would take in staff and money and what it might save, because the funding round closes in February 2027. A full evidence synthesis is not possible in that time, so I would like to run a rapid review.

The questions I think matter are these. Does pharmacist-led follow-up improve adherence to oral anticancer agents, and how was adherence measured? Does it reduce unplanned admissions or severe toxicity? What does it do to dose intensity, since earlier dose reductions for toxicity could protect patients but also reduce how much treatment they receive? How much pharmacist time does it take per patient? What does such a service need in money, and what is saved in admissions? And what do patients think of it? I know adherence can be measured in very different ways (pill counts, refill data, electronic caps, self-report) that give different answers, and that most studies are small.

Practical points. Two pharmacists can each give six hours a week to the review until the end of January, and our library can run searches. We cannot pay for translation. We want to include reports from other cancer centres and health technology assessment agencies, not only journal articles. The committee has asked that we separate evidence about adherence from evidence about harms and money, because last time a single summary figure was misleading. Our own admission and dispensing data are context only; they are not part of the review, and they cannot be shared outside the centre. We also need to be honest about what a rapid review cannot do: one screener for most records, and no full appraisal of every study.

Finally, the committee chair asked that the summary say clearly who the evidence does not cover: older patients living alone, patients who do not speak English, and patients far from the centre who cannot easily come in for a pharmacist review. About a fifth of our patients live more than 100 kilometres away, and a small but growing number start treatment with an interpreter present, so this matters for how a service would be designed as well as for whether it is funded. If the evidence turns out to be too thin for a firm answer, I would rather the committee hear that plainly, with the gaps named, than receive a confident summary built on a few small studies.
store.problem.constraints: No research budget. Two pharmacists for six hours a week each until 29 January 2027; the committee's funding round closes on 15 February 2027. Library searches are available; there is no budget for translation, so only English reports are eligible. Most records will be screened by one reviewer, with a second reviewer checking a 20 percent sample. Evidence about adherence must be reported separately from evidence about harms and about staff time and money; no single summary figure combining them. The centre's own admission and dispensing data are context only and cannot leave the centre. No contact with patients or prescribers for the review. The summary for the committee must be no longer than six pages plus appendices and must state which patient groups the evidence does not cover. Reports must be dated 2010 or later. Conference abstracts are eligible only when they report outcomes not available elsewhere. Any cost figure must be shown with the year and currency of the original report and must not be converted or inflated without stating the method. The review protocol, including these shortcuts, must be filed with the committee secretary before screening starts. Draft tables may be shared with the committee chair once, in the week of 11 January 2027.
